p.src: But Gael, the president of the glass company, was undoubtedly a friendly kappa. I often went with Gael to the club he belonged to, and spent many a pleasant evening there. One reason was that this club was far more comfortable than the Superman Club to which Tock belonged. Moreover, although Gael's conversation lacked the depth of the philosopher Mag's, it opened a wholly new world before me—a vast world. Gael would always talk cheerfully about all manner of things while stirring his cup of coffee with a spoon of pure gold. One particularly foggy evening, as I recall, I sat listening to Gael with a vase of winter roses between us. As I remember it, the room itself, as well as its chairs and tables, was in the Secession style: white, edged with slender lines of gold. His whole face beaming with a smile more self-satisfied than usual, Gael spoke, among other things, of the Quorax Party cabinet then in power. The word Quorax is merely a meaningless interjection, so there is no way to translate it except, perhaps, as “Oh!” At any rate, it was a political party that proclaimed, before all else, “the interests of all kappa.” “The man who controls the Quorax Party is the celebrated politician Loppe. It was Bismarck who said, ‘Honesty is the best diplomacy,’ was it not? But Loppe extends honesty to domestic government as well. …” “But Loppe's speeches…” “Now, please hear me out. Those speeches are, of course, ※ from beginning to end. But since everyone knows they are ※, in the end that amounts to honesty, does it not?

p.src: It is merely a prejudice peculiar to your kind to call it ※ without qualification. We kappa, unlike you people… But that is beside the point. What I wish to speak about is Loppe. Loppe controls the Quorax Party; and the man who controls Loppe in turn is the president of the Pou-Fou newspaper—this word “Pou-Fou” is likewise a meaningless interjection. If one absolutely had to translate it, there would be no choice but to render it as “Ah!”— Quiqui. Yet Quiqui cannot be said to be his own master either. The one who controls Quiqui is Gael, whom you see before you.”

p.src: “But—perhaps it is rude of me to say so, but the Poo-Foo News is a newspaper that sides with the workers, isn’t it? And yet its president, Quiqui, is also under your control…” “The reporters at the Poo-Foo News are, of course, on the workers’ side. But surely it is none other than Quiqui who controls those reporters. And Quiqui, in turn, cannot do without the backing of yours truly, Gael.” Still smiling as ever, Gael toyed with his solid-gold spoon. Looking at Gael like this, I found myself feeling sympathy for the reporters of the Poo-Foo News rather than hatred for Gael himself. Gael apparently sensed this sympathy at once in my silence, for he puffed out his enormous belly and said: “Oh, not all the reporters at the Poo-Foo News side with the workers. At any rate, we kappas take our own side before we take anyone else’s, you know. …But what makes matters still more troublesome is that even Gael himself is likewise under someone else’s control. Who do you suppose that person is? It is my wife. The beautiful Mrs. Gael.” Gael laughed loudly. “Surely that is a blessing rather than a hardship.” “In any case, I am content. But I can boast of it so freely only before you—only before you, who are not a kappa.” “Then, in short, it is Mrs. Gael who controls the Quorax cabinet.” “Well, I suppose one might put it that way. …But the war seven years ago, at least, must certainly have begun because of a certain female kappa.” “A war? Has there been a war in this country too?” “Indeed there has. And there is no telling when another may come in the future.

p.src: So long as there are neighboring countries, after all…” It was only then that I first learned that the land of the kappas was not nationally isolated. According to Gael’s explanation, the kappas always regarded the otters as their hypothetical enemy. Moreover, the otters were said to possess armaments in no way inferior to those of the kappas. I was more than a little interested in hearing about the kappas’ war against these otters. (For the existence of otters as formidable enemies of the kappas was apparently a new fact unknown not only to the author of A Brief Study of the Water Tiger, but even to Kunio Yanagita, author of A Collection of Tales from Mountain Islands.)

p.src: “Before that war broke out, both countries naturally remained vigilant, watching each other closely. That was because each feared the other equally. Then an otter living in this country paid a visit to a married kappa couple. The female kappa, as it happened, was plotting to kill her husband. Her husband was a profligate, you see. Besides, the life insurance on him may have offered her some temptation.” “Do you know the couple?” “Yes—no, I know only the male kappa. My wife and others speak of him as though he were a villain. But in my view, rather than a villain, he is a madman plagued by delusions of persecution, terrified of being caught by a female kappa. …So the female kappa put potassium cyanide into her husband’s cup of cocoa. But through some mistake or other, she served it to the visiting otter instead. The otter, of course, died. And then…” “And then war broke out?” “Yes. Unfortunately, that otter happened to have been decorated.” “Which side won the war?” “This country won, of course. Three hundred and sixty-nine thousand five hundred kappas gallantly gave their lives for that victory. But compared with the enemy country, a loss of that size was nothing at all. Nearly every piece of fur in this country is otter fur. During that war, besides manufacturing glass, I also sent coal cinders to the front.” “What did they use the coal cinders for?” “For food, of course. We kappas are bound to eat anything when we are hungry enough, you know.” “That is—please do not be angry.

p.src: “It is certainly a scandal in this country too. But if I speak of it openly myself, no one will make a scandal of it. As the philosopher Magg says, you know: ‘Speak of your own evil yourself; then evil shall vanish of itself.’ …Besides, I was fired not only by the prospect of profit but also by patriotism.” Just then, a waiter from the club came in. After bowing to Gael, the waiter spoke as though reciting a passage aloud. “There is a fire next door to your house.” “A f—a fire!” Gael sprang to his feet in alarm. Naturally, I stood up too. But the waiter, perfectly composed, added: “But it has already been put out.” Watching the waiter depart, Gael wore an expression halfway between laughter and tears. At the sight of that expression, I realized that until then I had hated the president of this glass company. But now Gael stood there neither as a great capitalist nor as anything else—only as an ordinary kappa. I took a winter rose from the vase and handed it to Gael. “Even though the fire has been put out, your wife must have had a terrible fright. Here, take this and go home.” “Thank you.” Gael clasped my hand. Then he suddenly grinned and said to me in a low voice: “The house next door belongs to me, you see. At least I can collect the fire insurance.” Even now I vividly remember Gael’s smile at that moment—a smile I could neither despise nor hate.
